title: HelperABISSHVocabulary
description: The shared vocabulary of the helper ABI's ssh service: what a credential reference is, what a probe can answer, what a destination is, which channels this generation opens, where a channel connects, and the identity of a remote listener. It declares $defs and nothing else, so one concept has one declaration (AD-8) — the same discipline identities.schema.json applies to sessions, applied to the second subject this wire grew (nocx-50w7p.2, extended by nocx-50w7p.3's proxied channels and nocx-50w7p.8's forwards). The service speaks in BOTH directions: `probe`, `open`, `close`, `forward` and `unforward` are forward ops the helper answers, and `secret`, `sign`, `verify-host-key` and `trust-host-key` are reverse ops the helper ASKS the coordinator, over the same connection its own request arrived on.

credential.description: An opaque handle on one stored credential, minted by the COORDINATOR and echoed back by the helper verbatim. The helper never interprets either field, and that is the whole authorization story on this wire: it cannot ask for material the coordinator did not name. PassphraseRef exists because a key and the passphrase that unlocks it are two stored secrets — resolving one where the other was meant is how a wrong-but-valid password gets tried against a server — and it is a REFERENCE and never material: the coordinator is the party that parses a private key, so a passphrase never reaches the helper at all.

ref.description: Names the material the credential's auth kind presents: the password for password auth, the private key for key auth.

passphraseRef.description: Names the passphrase of an encrypted key. Omitted for a password credential and for an unencrypted key.

authKind.description: How a probe authenticates, in a closed set. It is the COORDINATOR's decision and not the helper's: the coordinator is the party that knows which material it stored, and a helper that guessed would send the wrong rung of the ladder against somebody's machine.

purpose.description: What the material a helper asks for is FOR, in a closed set. The purpose is load-bearing rather than decorative: the read is stanced (internal/credential), so a password and a passphrase are resolved through different declarations, different reasons in the vault's own audit, and — where a profile carries policy — potentially different answers.

probeOutcome.description: The closed set of answers a probe can give. The spellings are ssh.ProbeOutcome's own, character for character: the coordinator classifies its own probes with ssh.ClassifyProbeError, and a second vocabulary for one fact is what AD-8 exists to prevent. `accepted` and `host-key-unknown` are different answers for the same reason a first connection is not a failure; `host-key-changed` is never conflated with it, because a changed key is the one signature of a machine in the middle. An unclassifiable failure is NOT a member here — it is a refusal of the op, so that 'the server refused this credential' and 'nobody knows what happened' stay apart.

hostKeyVerdict.description: The closed set of answers to 'what is this host key'. Naming three outcomes is what lets a helper — which links no knownhosts and has no callback to consult — act on the coordinator's answer: `trusted` is the absence of a host-key error in internal/ssh rather than a value it stores, and `changed` must never be answered as `unknown`, because accepting an unknown key and accepting a changed one are the two different decisions this vocabulary exists to keep apart.

identity.description: The credential a probe authenticates with, plus the PUBLIC half of a key credential. The public key is here rather than discovered by an op of its own because x/crypto/ssh's Signer interface answers PublicKey() BEFORE it asks for a signature: the helper must be able to declare which key it is offering before it can be asked to sign with it. It is public material — what the peer learns on the first packet — and the private half never crosses, which is why `sign` is exactly a challenge and a signature and why there is no empty-challenge sentinel hiding a discovery question inside a cryptographic one.

publicKey.description: The wire-format public key blob (RFC 4253 §6.6) as base64. Required for key auth — a helper asked to sign with a key it was not given would have to invent one — and absent for password auth.

destination.description: One RESOLVED destination: the address, the account and what to authenticate as. Its three parts are typed fields and never one `user@host:port` string, because a spelling would have to be parsed again on the far side by something that is not allowed to guess. The fields carry the same meaning probe.params gives its own copies of them, since a destination and a probe take the same three facts.

host.description: The dial target: an address, never an alias, because it is what the coordinator's own dial path resolved.

port.description: The resolved port. Required rather than defaulted here: a helper that picked 22 would be making a decision the profile already made.

channelKind.description: The closed set of PROXIED CHANNELS this generation opens. A kind names a protocol the helper itself implements; it is never a command, an argv or a free-form string list — host.Register refuses a bare []string outright (D3) — so a caller that wants a different channel adds a member here in a generation, with a protocol bump and a test. `sftp` is a session channel carrying the sftp SUBSYSTEM: the helper moves its bytes and does not speak the protocol, which is why pkg/sftp stays in the coordinator. `direct-tcpip` is a channel to an ADDRESS on the far side's network: it is the outbound half of a forward (-L) and of every SOCKS CONNECT, and it takes the `target` a subsystem open does not (nocx-50w7p.8).

channelId.description: One proxied channel's identity, minted by the helper and echoed verbatim by the coordinator. It is 32 hex characters — sixteen raw bytes on the data plane — and it is opaque in both directions: the coordinator never derives it and the helper never lets a caller choose it.

channelTarget.description: One address a channel is opened to, TYPED: two fields and never one "host:port" string, because a spelling would have to be parsed again on the far side by something that is not allowed to guess, and the one caller that legitimately carries a name rather than an address — a SOCKS CONNECT — still carries a NAME and a PORT. An IPv6 literal therefore crosses without brackets and is joined there.

host.description: The address or name to connect to, resolved on the FAR side. Empty is refused: an address that names nothing is not a target.

port.description: The port, 0-65535. 0 is legal on a LISTENER (the server allocates, and the answer carries what it allocated) and refused on a direct-tcpip target, where the far side would answer a connection to port 0 with a refusal of its own.

forwardId.description: One remote listener's identity, minted by the helper and echoed verbatim by the coordinator. It is a SEPARATE identity from a channel id rather than a second use of it: a channel is one stream somebody holds, a listener is the thing streams arrive ON, and the two are created and ended by different ops (`close` versus `unforward`). An id that could be either would make those interchangeable at the type level while meaning different things on the wire.

leaseId.description: One probe lease's identity: a reference the HELPER holds on a pooled ssh connection, minted by the helper and echoed verbatim by the coordinator. It is 32 hex characters, opaque in both directions, and it is neither a channelId nor a forwardId because the three name different things that different ops end: a channel is a stream somebody holds, a listener is the thing streams arrive on, and a lease is a REFERENCE to a connection held for as long as a caller wants commands run on the same transport.

probeRun.description: What every named probe needs and nothing more: the lease it runs on. It is one $def and not five inline fields so that 'a probe runs on a lease' has one declaration — and so a probe added later cannot grow a destination of its own, which would be a second way to say which connection this is.

lease.description: The reference this probe runs under. A lease this helper does not hold — a helper that restarted holds nothing — is refused as exec_lost rather than as a bad request: the connection it named is gone, which is the fact the caller acts on.

portProbe.description: One rung of port discovery's ladder, in the spellings internal/discovery reports as 'which dialect produced this sample'. A NAME and not a command: the caller chooses which probe to run, and the helper owns what it is (the text lives in internal/remoteprobe, which both ends link).

commandNamesPhase.description: Which half of the PATH enumeration to run, in a closed set of two. Two members rather than a flag because they are bounded differently: the cheap invalidation probe runs once per session, the full scan runs once per target and is shared.

probeExecResult.description: What every named probe answers: the captured streams, the remote exit status, and whether a capture bound was hit. It is ONE shape for all five probes deliberately — each caller classifies these facts its own way (discovery reads exit 127 as 'tool absent' and lsof's exit 1 as a valid empty sample, completion rejects an unframed answer, deploy refuses a nonzero status outright) and none of those are decisions the helper may take on the caller's behalf. `truncated` means the answer is a PREFIX: a partial table must never be read as a complete one, which for port discovery is the difference between 'no listeners' and 'I could not see them'.

stdout.description: The command's standard output, base64 in JSON ([]byte). Bounded by the helper's own capture cap; reaching it sets truncated rather than quietly returning less.

stderr.description: The command's standard error, same encoding. Carried rather than merged: completion rejects an unframed answer and discovery reports a bounded excerpt, and both need to see what the far side said.

exitStatus.description: The remote command's exit status, and it is an ANSWER rather than a failure: a missing tool exits 127, lsof exits 1 when nothing matched, a policy wrapper exits whatever it likes. The helper never folds a nonzero status into a refusal.

truncated.description: True when the capture bound was hit or the remote died mid-write — the payload is a prefix and must be treated as one.
